tagline: Mountain waterways and a hand-built toll road lead into Valle Crucis
intro: Mission Crossing follows curving NC 194 through the High Country, beside the Elk River, Craborchard Creek and the Watauga River. It is a North Carolina scenic byway connecting the Elk Park area with Vilas through Banner Elk and Valle Crucis. The state’s byway program selects roads to share North Carolina’s history, geography and culture. The riverbank alignment becomes markedly curvier between Elk Park and Vilas. One four-mile section of the former turnpike between Banner Elk and Valle Crucis Elementary School retains winding curves.

Part of this drive follows a roadbed built without machinery. Workers constructed the Valle Crucis, Shawneehaw and Elk Park Turnpike as a toll road in 1891–92, using hand labor. NC 194 took over the route from Elk Park to Vilas in 1930. The byway’s name refers to the Episcopal mission in Valle Crucis.

From the Elk Park end, follow the Elk River toward Banner Elk, where pedestrian crossings interrupt the drive. NC 184 branches toward the ski resorts on Beech and Sugar mountains. Beyond Banner Elk, the road follows Craborchard Creek from the county line into Valle Crucis and then the Watauga River through the community. The route reaches Vilas, where NC 194 joins US 321 and US 421.

moments.title: Old Turnpike Road
moments.text: The older roadbed incorporated into NC 194 belonged to the Valle Crucis, Shawneehaw and Elk Park Turnpike. Built in 1891–92 as a private toll road, it was constructed entirely by hand, without machinery. A four-mile section between Banner Elk and Valle Crucis Elementary School is known for its winding curves. The modern highway retains that older roadbed. Truck traffic between Banner Elk and Valle Crucis is directed to a separate route, with flashing signs warning drivers away from the main highway. The truck detour uses NC 184, NC 105 and Broadstone Road before rejoining NC 194 in Valle Crucis.

moments.title: Valle Crucis
moments.text: Three converging streams gave Valle Crucis its name: Vale of the Cross, in Latin. The community lies beside Dutch Creek and the Watauga River. The Episcopal mission’s school taught academic subjects and practical agriculture before closing in 1850. It reopened in 1895 under Bishop Joseph Blount Cheshire and the Rev. Milor Jones, with teachers and boarding students housed in the Mission House. The mission complex includes the stone, Gothic Revival Church of the Holy Cross, a cemetery, barns and an apple orchard. Its church cornerstone was laid in 1924. The mission is also known as the Valle Crucis Conference Center.

moments.title: Mast General Store
moments.text: Henry Taylor built the original store in 1882 and opened it in 1883. W.W. Mast bought a half interest in 1897 and the rest in 1913, giving the business its present name. Three generations of the family kept it until its sale in 1973. The store closed in 1977 and reopened in 1980 after John and Faye Cooper bought it. The Valle Crucis building entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. In 1996, ownership changed again: the company became an employee-owned business. It continues to house the community’s post office.
